q: What is the correct order of the parts of the human alimentary canal?
o: Mouth → oesophagus → pharynx → stomach → small intestine → large intestine
Mouth → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → small intestine → large intestine
Mouth → pharynx → stomach → oesophagus → large intestine → small intestine
Mouth → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach → large intestine → small intestine
x: Food passes from the mouth through the pharynx into the oesophagus, then the stomach, the small intestine and finally the large intestine, ending at the anus.

q: The wall of the alimentary canal has four layers. Their correct order from the inside (lumen) outwards is:
x: The mucosa lines the lumen, the submucosa lies beneath it, then the muscle layers (muscularis), and the serosa forms the outer covering.

q: Which layer of the gut wall is made of loose connective tissue carrying the larger blood vessels, lymph vessels and a nerve network?
x: The submucosa is connective tissue rich in blood and lymph vessels and nerves that supply the mucosa. The mucosa is the inner lining with glands, and the muscularis contains the muscle layers.

q: Most of the gut has circular and longitudinal muscle layers. The stomach wall is special because it has an additional:
x: The stomach has an extra inner oblique layer of smooth muscle, which helps it churn food and mix it with gastric juice.

q: A complete set of permanent teeth in an adult human has:
x: The full adult set has 32 teeth: 8 incisors, 4 canines, 8 premolars and 12 molars (including the wisdom teeth). The milk set has 20.

q: The chisel-shaped front teeth used for biting and cutting food are the:
x: Incisors have sharp, flat edges for cutting. Canines are pointed for tearing, and premolars and molars have broad surfaces for grinding.

q: How many milk (deciduous) teeth does a child normally have?
x: The milk set has 20 teeth, which are later replaced by the 32 permanent teeth.

q: Which type of tooth is present in the permanent set but absent from the milk set?
x: The milk set has incisors, canines and molars but no premolars. In the permanent set, premolars grow in place of the milk molars, and new permanent molars erupt behind them.

q: The crown of a tooth is covered by the hardest substance in the body, which is:
x: Enamel, mostly calcium salts, covers the crown and is the hardest tissue in the body. Dentine lies under it and cement covers the root.

q: The main bulk of a tooth, lying beneath the enamel and around the pulp cavity, is made of:
x: Dentine is a bone-like tissue that forms most of the tooth. It is covered by enamel on the crown and by cement on the root.

q: The pulp cavity at the centre of a tooth contains:
x: The pulp is soft tissue with blood vessels that nourish the tooth and nerves that give sensation. Enamel and dentine form the hard outer parts.

q: How many pairs of major salivary glands pour saliva into the human mouth?
x: There are three pairs: parotid, submandibular and sublingual glands.

q: The largest salivary glands, lying just in front of and below the ears, are the:
x: The parotid glands are the largest salivary glands and lie in front of the ears. Submandibular glands are under the lower jaw and sublingual glands under the tongue.

q: The pharynx is a passage for both food and air. During swallowing, food is stopped from entering the windpipe by the:
x: When we swallow, the larynx rises and the epiglottis, a flap of cartilage, covers the glottis so food passes into the oesophagus and not into the trachea.

q: On its way from the chest to the stomach, the oesophagus passes through the:
x: The oesophagus runs down through the thorax behind the trachea and pierces the diaphragm to join the stomach in the abdomen.

q: The ring of muscle that guards the opening between the oesophagus and the stomach is the:
x: The cardiac sphincter, at the cardiac end of the stomach, opens to let food in and closes to stop acid going back into the oesophagus. The pyloric sphincter is at the other end of the stomach.

q: The pyloric sphincter controls the passage of:
o: Bolus from the oesophagus into the stomach
Bile from the gall bladder into the duodenum
Chyme from the stomach into the duodenum
Faeces from the rectum into the anal canal
x: The pyloric sphincter lies between the stomach and the duodenum and releases chyme into the small intestine a little at a time.

q: The dome-shaped part of the stomach that bulges upwards beside the entry of the oesophagus is the:
x: The fundus is the upper rounded part of the stomach, often filled with gas. The body is the main middle part, and the pyloric region leads to the duodenum.

q: When the stomach is empty, its inner lining is thrown into folds called:
x: Rugae are folds of the stomach mucosa and submucosa that flatten out as the stomach fills, letting it stretch. Villi and microvilli are features of the small intestine.

q: The three parts of the small intestine, in the order food passes through them, are:
x: Chyme leaves the stomach into the duodenum, then passes through the jejunum and the ileum before reaching the large intestine.

q: Which part of the small intestine is the longest?
x: The ileum is the longest part of the small intestine. The duodenum is the short first part (about 25 cm), and the caecum belongs to the large intestine.

q: The ducts carrying bile and pancreatic juice open into the:
x: The common bile duct and the pancreatic duct join and open into the duodenum, so bile and pancreatic juice act on chyme as soon as it leaves the stomach.

q: In the centre of each villus of the small intestine there is a blind-ended lymph vessel called a:
x: Each villus has a central lacteal surrounded by a network of blood capillaries. The lacteal carries absorbed fat away in the lymph.

q: The 'brush border' on the epithelial cells lining the small intestine is formed by:
x: Each absorptive cell carries thousands of tiny projections of its cell membrane, the microvilli, which look like a brush under the microscope. Villi are larger, many-celled projections.

q: The vermiform appendix is a small blind tube attached to the:
x: The appendix projects from the caecum, the pouch at the start of the large intestine where the ileum joins it.

q: Which is the correct order of the parts of the colon, starting from the caecum?
x: From the caecum the colon goes up on the right (ascending), across the abdomen (transverse), down on the left (descending) and then forms the S-shaped sigmoid colon, which leads to the rectum.

q: The last part of the large intestine, where faeces are stored until they are passed out, is the:
x: Faeces collect in the rectum until egestion through the anal canal and anus. The caecum is the first part of the large intestine, the appendix is a blind tube attached to the caecum, and the ileum belongs to the small intestine.

q: The largest gland in the human body is the:
x: The liver is the largest gland in the body. It lies in the upper right part of the abdomen under the diaphragm.

q: Which statement about the gall bladder is correct?
o: It stores and concentrates bile made by the liver
It secretes lipase into the duodenum
x: Bile is made continuously by liver cells; the gall bladder stores it and concentrates it by absorbing water, then releases it into the duodenum after a meal.

q: The pancreas lies:
o: Above the diaphragm, beside the heart
Inside the wall of the stomach
Beside the rectum in the pelvis
Behind the stomach, with its head in the loop of the duodenum
x: The pancreas is a long gland lying behind the stomach; its head sits in the C-shaped curve of the duodenum, into which its duct opens.

q: The anus is guarded by two sphincters. Which statement about them is correct?
o: The internal one is smooth and involuntary; the external one is skeletal and voluntary
Both are made of smooth muscle and are involuntary
Both are made of skeletal muscle and are voluntary
The internal one is skeletal and voluntary; the external one is smooth and involuntary
x: The internal anal sphincter is smooth muscle under involuntary control, while the external sphincter is skeletal muscle under voluntary control, which is why egestion can be delayed.

q: Which of the following is NOT a part of the alimentary canal itself?
x: The pancreas is an accessory gland that pours its juice into the duodenum through a duct; food never passes through it. The jejunum, caecum and pharynx are all parts of the food tube.

q: Salivary amylase begins the digestion of:
x: Salivary amylase (ptyalin) breaks starch down into the disaccharide maltose. Saliva has no enzyme for proteins or fats.

q: Salivary amylase stops working soon after the food mixes with gastric juice because:
o: The stomach's acidic pH inactivates it
x: Salivary amylase works best near neutral pH. The hydrochloric acid in gastric juice lowers the pH strongly, which inactivates the enzyme.

q: The mucus in saliva helps digestion mainly by:
o: Lubricating food and binding it into a bolus for swallowing
Killing all bacteria in the mouth
x: Mucus moistens and lubricates chewed food and holds it together as a soft bolus that slides easily down the oesophagus. Starch digestion is the job of amylase.

q: Peristalsis is best described as:
o: Waves of muscle contraction that push food along the gut
Swallowing of food by voluntary action of the tongue
Absorption of digested food through villi
Churning of food by the teeth
x: Peristalsis is a wave of contraction of the smooth muscle in the gut wall that moves food along the alimentary canal, from the oesophagus to the rectum.

q: During peristalsis in the oesophagus, the bolus is pushed forward because:
o: Longitudinal muscle contracts behind it and circular muscle relaxes everywhere
Circular muscle contracts in front of the bolus and relaxes behind it
Circular muscle contracts behind the bolus and relaxes in front of it
Skeletal muscle of the diaphragm pushes on it
x: Contraction of circular muscle just behind the bolus squeezes it forward, while the region ahead relaxes (and longitudinal muscle shortens it) to receive it. Contraction in front would block the bolus.

q: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach is secreted by the:
x: Parietal or oxyntic cells of the gastric glands secrete hydrochloric acid. Chief cells secrete pepsinogen and mucous cells secrete mucus.

q: Pepsinogen is secreted by which cells of the gastric glands?
x: Chief cells release the inactive enzyme pepsinogen. Parietal cells make the acid that converts it to pepsin.

q: Food leaves the stomach as chyme, a thick semi-liquid. Chyme is formed mainly by:
o: Bile emulsifying the food while it is in the stomach
Absorption of most digested nutrients through the stomach wall
Churning by the muscular stomach wall, mixing food with gastric juice
Salivary amylase digesting proteins in the stomach
x: The muscle layers of the stomach wall churn the food and mix it with gastric juice, turning it into semi-liquid chyme. Bile acts in the duodenum, not the stomach, and little absorption takes place in the stomach.

q: Pepsin acts on proteins in the stomach and breaks them into:
x: Pepsin splits long protein chains into shorter polypeptides. Final breakdown to amino acids happens in the small intestine by trypsin and peptidases.

q: Which of the following is NOT a function of hydrochloric acid in the stomach?
o: Killing many bacteria taken in with food
Digesting fats into fatty acids and glycerol
Providing an acidic pH for pepsin
x: Hydrochloric acid does not digest fats; fats are digested mainly by lipase in the small intestine. The acid kills microbes, activates pepsinogen and gives the low pH pepsin needs.

q: The stomach normally does not digest its own wall even though it contains pepsin and strong acid. This is because:
o: A thick mucus layer covers the lining, and the enzyme is secreted in an inactive form
The stomach wall contains no protein
Pepsin only acts at neutral pH
Bile flows back into the stomach and neutralises it
x: A layer of mucus protects the lining from acid and pepsin, and secreting pepsinogen rather than pepsin prevents the cells that make it from digesting themselves. When this protection fails, a peptic ulcer can form.

q: The hormone gastrin is released when food enters the stomach. Its main effect is to:
x: Gastrin is made by cells in the stomach wall (mainly the pyloric region) and carried in the blood back to the gastric glands, increasing the secretion of gastric juice.

q: When acidic chyme enters the duodenum, the hormone secretin is released. Secretin mainly stimulates the pancreas to secrete:
o: A watery juice rich in bicarbonate
x: Secretin from the duodenal wall makes the pancreas release a bicarbonate-rich juice that neutralises the acid chyme. Pepsinogen and acid come from the stomach.

q: After a fatty meal, the gall bladder contracts and releases bile. The hormone responsible is:
x: Cholecystokinin is released by the duodenum when fat and protein arrive; it makes the gall bladder contract and the pancreas release its enzymes.

q: Which hormone is correctly matched with the place where it is made?
x: Gastrin is made by the stomach wall, while secretin and cholecystokinin are both made by the wall of the duodenum. The gall bladder and pancreas are targets of these hormones, not their sources.

q: Bile helps in the digestion of fats by:
o: Breaking fats into fatty acids and glycerol
Absorbing fats into the blood directly
x: Bile contains no enzymes. Its bile salts break fat into tiny droplets (emulsification), giving lipase a much larger surface to act on.

q: Bile pigments such as bilirubin are produced from the breakdown of:
o: Haemoglobin of old red blood cells
x: Old red blood cells are broken down and the haem part of their haemoglobin is converted into bile pigments, which the liver excretes in bile; they give faeces their colour.

q: Which of the following is NOT a function of the liver?
o: Forming urea from excess amino acids
x: Insulin is secreted by the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas. The liver stores glycogen, deaminates amino acids to form urea, detoxifies substances and makes bile.

q: Pancreatic lipase digests:
o: Fats into fatty acids and glycerol
x: Lipase hydrolyses fats (triglycerides) into fatty acids and glycerol. Its action is speeded up by bile, which emulsifies the fat first.

q: Trypsinogen from the pancreas is converted into active trypsin in the duodenum by:
x: Enterokinase (enteropeptidase), made by the lining of the small intestine, activates trypsinogen to trypsin. Hydrochloric acid activates pepsinogen in the stomach.

q: The bicarbonate in pancreatic juice is important for digestion in the duodenum because it:
o: Neutralises acid chyme so pancreatic and intestinal enzymes can work
x: Chyme arrives very acidic. Bicarbonate neutralises it, giving the slightly alkaline pH at which pancreatic and intestinal enzymes work best, and pepsin stops acting.

q: The endocrine part of the pancreas, which secretes insulin and glucagon into the blood, consists of the:
x: Scattered islets of Langerhans make insulin and glucagon and release them into the blood. The acini are the exocrine part that makes digestive enzymes.

q: The enzyme maltase in the small intestine converts maltose into:
x: Maltose is made of two glucose units, so maltase splits it into two glucose molecules. Sucrase gives glucose and fructose and lactase gives glucose and galactose.

q: Sucrose (cane sugar) is digested in the small intestine by:
x: Sucrase splits sucrose into glucose and fructose. Each disaccharide has its own enzyme in the intestinal lining.

q: Proteins are finally absorbed from the small intestine in the form of:
x: Pepsin, trypsin and peptidases together break proteins down to amino acids, which are small enough to be absorbed into the blood capillaries of the villi.

q: After absorption, the products of fat digestion are carried away from the villi mainly through the:
x: Fatty acids and glycerol recombine into fat inside the intestinal cells and pass into the lacteals, so they travel first in the lymph before entering the blood.

q: Glucose and amino acids absorbed into the blood capillaries of the villi are first carried to the:
o: Liver, through the hepatic portal vein
x: Capillaries from the intestine drain into the hepatic portal vein, which takes absorbed sugars and amino acids to the liver to be processed before they reach the general circulation. Fats travel instead in lymph to the thoracic duct.

q: Villi and microvilli in the small intestine help absorption mainly by:
x: Folds, villi and microvilli together greatly enlarge the surface of the small intestine, so digested food is absorbed quickly.

q: The main function of the large intestine (colon) is to:
o: Absorb water and salts from the undigested remains
x: The colon absorbs most of the remaining water and mineral salts, turning the liquid contents into semi-solid faeces. It secretes no digestive enzymes.

q: Bacteria living in the human large intestine produce a vitamin that the body absorbs. This vitamin is:
x: Bacteria in the colon make vitamin K (and some B vitamins), which is absorbed. Vitamin K is needed for blood clotting.

q: A peptic ulcer develops in the stomach or duodenum when:
o: Too much water is absorbed by the colon
Salivary amylase digests the stomach wall
The protective mucus fails, so acid and pepsin erode the lining
x: A peptic ulcer is an open sore that forms when acid and pepsin wear away the lining; the mucus barrier is often damaged by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori. Salivary amylase does not act on the stomach wall.

q: Diarrhoea can quickly lead to dehydration because:
o: The colon absorbs too much water
Food passes through the colon too fast for enough water to be absorbed
x: In diarrhoea the contents move rapidly through the large intestine, so little water is reabsorbed and much water and salt are lost in watery faeces.

q: A person eats very little fibre and often delays going to the toilet. Why does this tend to cause constipation?
o: Faeces move too fast, so too little water is absorbed
Fibre is needed to make bile
Lack of fibre stops gastric juice secretion
Faeces move slowly, so too much water is absorbed and they become hard
x: Fibre adds bulk that stimulates peristalsis. Without it, and with delay, faeces stay longer in the colon, more water is absorbed, and they become hard and dry. Fast movement with little water absorbed is diarrhoea.
